domains.name: Data
questions: We have agreed systems of record for finance, HR/payroll and core service data.
Every key dataset has a named owner who is responsible for its quality.
Our data is classified by sensitivity (public, internal, confidential, regulated).
Staff can get reliable reports from ERP/HRIS without manual spreadsheet cleanup.
moves: Name a system of record for finance, HR/payroll and each core service dataset, and publish the list.
Assign a data owner to every key dataset, with quality as part of their role.
Start a simple four-level data classification and tag your top 20 datasets first.

domains.name: Policy and Governance
questions: We have a short written AI policy covering approved tools, prohibited uses and data handling.
A named leader owns AI adoption, with authority across departments (not only IT).
We review AI tools for security, privacy, records retention and accessibility before use.
We have a process to approve, monitor and retire AI initiatives.
moves: Adopt a 2-page AI policy: approved tools, prohibited uses, data handling, who to ask.
Name an AI lead with cross-department authority and a small working group.
Use a one-page tool review checklist covering security, privacy, records, accessibility and cost model.

domains.name: People and Literacy
questions: Leadership has explained to staff why we are using AI and how it affects their roles.
Most staff have completed basic AI training on our approved tools.
Staff know what data they may and may not put into AI tools.
We have power users in departments who help others adopt AI.
moves: Have leadership explain the why: capacity goes back to service, not cuts by default.
Run role-based training for leaders, power users and all staff on approved tools and safe data use.
Recruit one power user per department and give them time to help peers.

domains.name: Use Cases and ROI
questions: We have a ranked list of workflows where AI could save time or improve service.
Each AI initiative has a baseline measured before it starts (hours, backlog, errors, cycle time).
Each initiative has an owner, a KPI and a decision date to continue or stop.
We can show measured results from at least one AI use case to council, board or leadership.
moves: Collect pain points from departments and score them by impact and effort; pick 3 to 5.
Measure a baseline before any initiative starts: hours, backlog, errors or cycle time.
Give every initiative a one-line card: baseline, owner, KPI, target and a kill-or-fund date.

domains.name: Systems and Integration
questions: Our ERP, HRIS and key service systems are current, supported versions.
Core systems expose APIs or integrations that AI tools can use securely.
We use enterprise AI licenses with business data protections (not personal accounts).
We can budget AI costs predictably (fixed fees, usage caps or monitoring).
moves: Inventory ERP, HRIS and service systems with version and support status; plan upgrades for anything unsupported.
Document which core systems have secure APIs and close the integration gaps that block priority use cases.
Move staff off personal AI accounts to enterprise licenses, and set usage caps or monitoring for cost.

stages.name: Ground Truth
stages.desc: AI use is informal and unmanaged. Data lives in silos and spreadsheets, and no system of record is agreed for key data.

stages.name: Guardrails
stages.desc: Leadership has said yes to AI with rules. Data classification has started and data quality issues are documented.

stages.name: Assisted Work
stages.desc: Staff use approved AI for drafting, summarizing and analysis. First quick wins are measured against baselines.

stages.name: Connected Workflows
stages.desc: AI is built into processes, with ERP, HRIS and service systems integrated and data governance run as a routine.

stages.name: Autonomous Workflows
stages.desc: Supervised agents complete multi-step work across systems with human approval points, monitoring and rollback.
